clue.text: Rightful view of old acrostic features

definitions.meaning: in English law, windows that have enjoyed daylight for twenty years or more gain a legal right not to have their view blocked
the solutions in an acrostic puzzle are called lights, so those of an antique acrostic are aged lights

explanation.surface: A lawyer weighs the fair outlook from a house with an antique puzzle carved on its walls.
explanation.walkthrough: The legal term sits in old English property law; the second reading treats 'lights' as the puzzle word for answers and 'ancient' as old.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses rest on the word lights: legally protected windows, and the entries of an antique word puzzle.

clue.text: Crab Currer a la carte?

parts.note: a crab is a kind of apple, the small sour crab apple
Currer Bell was the pen name of the novelist Charlotte Brontë

explanation.surface: Someone orders a grumpy author's dish straight off the menu.
explanation.walkthrough: Crab apple gives the fruit; Currer Bell was the pseudonym Charlotte Brontë published Jane Eyre under, so Currer stands for her first name. The '?' warns that the definition is only an example of something ordered from a menu.
explanation.definitionFit: This baked pudding of fruit in buttered bread is a dish one might pick from a restaurant menu.

clue.text: Big win at piquet, about everything wagered

parts.note: ca, short for circa, is Latin for about
the pot is the whole sum staked in a game

explanation.surface: A card player stakes everything and takes the whole game.
explanation.walkthrough: Piquet is an old two-player card game; taking every trick in a hand there has its own name.
explanation.definitionFit: In piquet, winning all twelve tricks of a deal is scored as this sweep.

clue.text: Well-fed leaders of the opening chorus

definitions.meaning: from the proverb that the first riser catches the worm, so is well fed
the birds that start the dawn chorus at first light

explanation.surface: The well-fed leads of a show sing its first number.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'opening chorus' looks theatrical but is the dawn chorus of birdsong; the 'well-fed' sense comes from the saying about catching the worm.
explanation.definitionFit: Proverbially the first to rise catch the worm, and the first songbirds start the dawn singing.

clue.text: Leaders in tragedy and one that plays a part on the farm

definitions.text: Leaders in tragedy and one that plays a part on the farm

indicators.note: the leading letters of the word tragedy are taken, here the opening pair

parts.note: an actor is someone who plays a role

explanation.surface: Stars of a tragedy and a supporting player turn up at a farm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaders in' takes the first two letters of 'tragedy'; the whole clue then reads as a description of the farm machine, which plays its part in farm work.
explanation.definitionFit: The engine that pulls ploughs and trailers does its share of agricultural labour.

clue.text: Mark clearly where scriveners take a dip

parts.note: to ink is to mark something in ink
well, in the sense of distinctly or properly

explanation.surface: Instructions to write boldly where clerks dip their pens.
explanation.walkthrough: A scrivener is an old word for a professional clerk or scribe, who dipped a pen into a pot set in the desk.
explanation.definitionFit: Desks once held a pot of writing fluid into which clerks dipped their pens.

clue.text: Victor appears to embrace the air

parts.note: to hug is to embrace
O stands for nothing, as in thin air or empty space

explanation.surface: A winner seems to hug the empty air in celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Victor' looks like a winner but is a first name: the French novelist of Les Misérables.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of Les Misérables had Victor as his first name.

clue.text: Lyrical series proposed for Daisy Bell?

definitions.text: Lyrical series proposed for Daisy Bell?

parts.words: Lyrical series proposed for Daisy Bell?
parts.note: a set of songs read cryptically: the Daisy Bell music-hall song proposes marriage on a bicycle built for two

explanation.surface: A suggested programme of songs for a singer called Daisy Bell.
explanation.walkthrough: Daisy Bell is the old music-hall song ending 'on the seat of a bicycle made for two', so a song and its bike go together.
explanation.definitionFit: A connected series of songs set to poems, here split as a song plus a bike.

clue.text: How to secure stable door before the horse decides to do so

definitions.text: How to secure stable door before the horse decides to do so

parts.words: How to secure stable door before the horse decides to do so
parts.note: fitting a sliding bar to the stall door, before the animal takes the chance to dash off

explanation.surface: Advice on fastening the stable before the horse escapes.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb about shutting the stable door after the horse has bolted is turned round: fit a bolt in advance, before the horse itself bolts.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to run off suddenly, and literally a bolt is a bar that fastens a door.

clue.text: Reading for the daily help

parts.note: a daily is a newspaper published every day
to back is to support or help

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a book to read while hiring a daily cleaner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The daily help' suggests a cleaner, but 'the daily' is a newspaper and 'help' is to back it.
explanation.definitionFit: A soft-covered book is something one takes up for reading.

clue.text: Italian city to feed Marie- Antoinette's hungry masses?

definitions.meaning: a port in Liguria in north-west Italy

definitions.text: to feed Marie- Antoinette's hungry masses?
definitions.meaning: a rich fruit cake, the kind of cake the queen supposedly told the starving poor to eat

explanation.surface: A city is offered to feed the starving crowds the French queen dismissed.
explanation.walkthrough: Marie Antoinette is said to have answered the hungry poor with 'Let them eat cake'; this city also names a rich fruit cake.
explanation.definitionFit: A port in northern Italy, and a rich fruit cake named after it.

clue.text: Record of two points, and four at Twickenham

parts.note: E and N are two compass points, east and north
a try in rugby was then worth four points; Twickenham is the English rugby ground

explanation.surface: A rugby scorer notes two points and then four more at the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Twickenham is the home of English rugby union, where a try scored four points when this puzzle ran. The 'two points' are compass points, not a score.
explanation.definitionFit: An item written into a register or ledger is a recorded item.

clue.text: A half-thousand the objective

parts.note: the first half of the word thousand is an old second-person pronoun, and this asks for its objective case form

explanation.surface: A target of five hundred is set as the aim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-thousand' looks like 500 but means the first half of the word, THOU; 'objective' looks like an aim but is the grammatical case, the archaic form used after verbs.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic pronoun used as object, as in 'I love thee', is the objective case of thou.

clue.text: Came out top

indicators.note: out says the letters of came are thrown out of order and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone finished in first place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges CAME; 'Came out top' reads as winning.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest point or peak is the top.

clue.text: Accommodation for a floating population?

parts.note: a floating population usually means people who move about, but here the homes literally float on water

explanation.surface: Housing is sought for a shifting, transient population.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Floating population' is a phrase for transient residents; read literally, the people live afloat, moored on rivers and canals.
explanation.definitionFit: Vessels moored and fitted out as dwellings house people living on the water.

clue.text: Not so easy eating one that's' tougher

indicators.note: eating means one word swallows another, holding it inside itself

parts.note: harder means less easy
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A diet grows harder to follow when it toughens you up.
explanation.definitionFit: More robust and resilient, as a hardier plant survives frost.

clue.text: From points where acorns fell (but not these flowering ones)

parts.note: a compass rose is the card showing the points of the compass
acorns drop from oak trees

explanation.surface: A naturalist notes where acorns dropped, adding that flowering shrubs were not the source.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'points' are compass points, drawn on a rose; the bracket then says these flowering ones are not where acorns came from.
explanation.definitionFit: Roses grown on a single tall stem are flowering shrubs trained like small trees.

clue.text: Prince of beasts?

parts.note: if the lion is king of beasts, its young son would be the prince

explanation.surface: A title asks who is heir among the animals.
explanation.walkthrough: The lion is traditionally the king of beasts, so the king's son is a prince.
explanation.definitionFit: The young of the king of beasts would be heir, like a prince to the throne.

clue.text: Desires a new shape in stays

indicators.note: giving the word desires a new shape means rearranging its letters

explanation.surface: Desires take a new form while one is laced into stays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stays' looks like a corset but is the verb: lives or remains.
explanation.definitionFit: To dwell or live somewhere is to stay there.

clue.text: Her best concoction a drink

indicators.note: a concoction is a mixture, so the letters of her best are mixed up

explanation.surface: She mixes up her best concoction to drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A fizzy fruit cordial, sometimes a sweet powder, was drunk as a refreshing beverage.

clue.text: This Scotsman wrote of the lexicographer…

definitions.text: This Scotsman wrote of the lexicographer…

parts.words: This Scotsman wrote of the lexicographer
parts.note: James, the Scots lawyer who wrote the great Life of Samuel Johnson, the dictionary maker

explanation.surface: A Scot writes about a dictionary maker.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Johnson compiled the 1755 Dictionary; his biographer was a Scot. The ellipsis runs into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: James, the Scottish lawyer, wrote the famous biography of Samuel Johnson.

clue.text: City seventy miles from the nursery

definitions.meaning: the ancient capital on the Euphrates
the nursery rhyme asks how many miles to this city and answers threescore and ten

explanation.surface: A city lies seventy miles from the nursery.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme runs 'How many miles to Babylon? Threescore miles and ten', which is seventy miles.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Mesopotamian capital, and the place in the old nursery rhyme.

clue.text: … who defined this grain as his people's support

definitions.text: … who defined this grain as his people's support

parts.words: who defined this grain as his people's support
parts.note: Johnson's dictionary called this cereal one given to horses in England but which in Scotland supports the people

explanation.surface: The Scot's subject defined a cereal as what fed the Scots.
explanation.walkthrough: Continuing from 20 across: Johnson's Dictionary famously defined this grain as food for horses in England but for people in Scotland, a dig Boswell's countrymen remembered.
explanation.definitionFit: The cereal grain used for porridge, defined by Johnson as Scottish people's food.

clue.text: Word from some lover belatedly

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Word arrives at last from a tardy sweetheart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' points inside 'lover belatedly'.
explanation.definitionFit: A doing word is a part of speech, a kind of word.

clue.text: "Drest in a little authority " (Meas for Meas)

definitions.text: "Drest in a little authority " (Meas for Meas)

parts.words: "Drest in a little authority " (Meas for Meas)
parts.note: fill the gap in Isabella's line in Shakespeare's Measure for Measure about proud man's short-lived power

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Isabella's speech in Measure for Measure reads 'Dress'd in a little ___ authority'; the missing word means short-lived.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing adjective means short or fleeting, as man's passing power is.

clue.text: Accustom to being nearly ruined perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters given are only one possible arrangement of them
nearly means the word ruined loses its final letter

explanation.surface: Someone gets used to being almost ruined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nearly' drops the D of 'ruined', and 'perhaps' rearranges RUINE.
explanation.definitionFit: To harden someone to something unpleasant is to make them used to it.

clue.text: He appears to race in circles

indicators.note: in places the race inside the circles

parts.note: two O shapes look like two circles
the TT is the Tourist Trophy motorcycle race on the Isle of Man

explanation.surface: A man seems to drive round and round in circles.
explanation.walkthrough: The TT is the Isle of Man motorbike race; 'He' is a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's first name, so a male person.

clue.text: Crime by the short measure

parts.note: ft is the short form of foot, a unit of length

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper commits a crime by giving short measure.
explanation.walkthrough: Short measure suggests cheating a customer, but here it is the abbreviated unit.
explanation.definitionFit: Stealing is an offence against the law.

clue.text: Invest to be member of football organization?

parts.note: a leaguer is a member of a league, such as the Football League

explanation.surface: A club aims to be a member of the Football League.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Invest' looks financial but is the military sense: surround with troops.
explanation.definitionFit: To invest a town is the old military sense of besieging it.

clue.text: No dessert ? What nonsense! But pleasantly 23

definitions.meaning: lacking a pudding is being short of something sweet, and the exclamation fits a protest
23 across is a word for short, so pleasantly short

explanation.surface: Someone protests at being denied pudding, though briefly and agreeably.
explanation.walkthrough: One reading: no dessert means being short of a sweet, a dinner protest. The other is the idiom for pleasantly concise; 23 across supplies the word for concise.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something agreeably concise, short yet pleasing.
